claims.text: Anomalous high-temperature mechanical behavior in refractory HEAs is primarily caused by heterogeneous lattice distortions that modify dislocation core energies.
Heterogeneous lattice distortion promotes thermally activated edge-dislocation activity, including thermal super-jogging, over screw-dominated plasticity.
Edge-dislocation-dominated activity causes unusually sustained high-temperature yield strength or a yield-strength plateau.
The altered dislocation activity produces a modified high-temperature elastic response.
The proposed materials are cold-rolled and annealed, equiatomic, single-phase BCC polycrystalline sheets.
Minor additions of HCP-prone elements such as Ti, Zr, or Hf increase lattice distortion in a refractory BCC HEA.
Using identical cold-rolling and annealing routes for the two alloys isolates lattice heterogeneity as the governing variable.
The controlled comparison should use tensile testing and in-situ TEM or neutron diffraction from 673 to 1073 K under inert atmosphere at a constant moderate strain rate.
Lattice-distortion heterogeneity creates local variations in dislocation core energies.
The local energy landscape favors edge-dislocation nucleation and activation.
Increased lattice distortion lowers the barrier for edge-dislocation motion relative to screw-dislocation motion.
Thermal super-jogging impedes conventional thermally activated softening.
The distortion-enhanced alloy will soften less and display a yield-strength plateau at high temperature.
The distortion-enhanced alloy will exhibit more edge dislocations and structures such as multiple kinks or jogs.
The baseline all-BCC refractory HEA will undergo conventional thermal softening with screw-dislocation-dominated activity.
VNbMoTaW has minimal lattice distortion and can serve as the conventional-softening baseline.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation and extraneous phase transformations during testing.
Comparable grain size, impurity content, and processing-induced defect populations are required for attributing differences to lattice distortion.
The quantitative effects of distortion on activation energies and dislocation dynamics remain uncertain.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified alloy shows neither a yield-strength plateau nor enhanced edge-dislocation signatures and both alloys exhibit similar thermal softening.

contradictions.description: Both variants are described as equiatomic, while the modified variant is produced by a minor elemental addition without specifying a compensating substitution; a simple addition would generally make the modified alloy non-equiatomic.
